title: Anthropic Only Major Lab to Confirm Recursive AI Coding at NYC Hearing

tickers.name: Alphabet Inc. Class A Common Stock
Meta Platforms, Inc. Class A Common Stock

summary:
OpenAI and Google representatives declined to state whether their systems produce code for next-generation versions of themselves during an Oct. 5 safety inquiry. Anthropic was the only leading firm to acknowledge that its artificial intelligence utilizes a recursive loop, where a model's own output is used in subsequent training rounds to produce a more intelligent successor. Representatives from Meta were unable to say if their models self-generate code as members of the New York City Council questioned the companies on how they quantify risk and whether they have undisclosed cyber incidents.

Former researchers from Anthropic and OpenAI testified that automating AI research is now the primary goal of the industry, with milestones for an automated researcher reaching 2027 or 2028 on track or ahead of schedule. Jacob Coxon, a former Anthropic employee, stated the majority of code is already AI-written without sufficient human review. These disclosures occur as all 51 council members weigh a bill to outlaw the sale of AI models in the city without outside validation, which would include $25K fines per unvalidated deployment and a mandatory human-operated shutdown capability.

selectedTweets.text:
Looks like, only Anthropic confirmed to NYC lawmakers that its models write code for smarter successors.

At the Council’s October 5 hearing, a New York City Council member was questioning them about a loop where a model’s own code runs in the next training round and produces a smarter model.

OpenAI and Google avoided a yes or no by questioning whether the council member’s description matched their own technical definition of recursive self-improvement

Meta’s representative couldn’t say whether its model self-generates code.

selectedTweets.text:
Jacob Coxon (Anthropic researcher whol quit a few days back) during the New York City Council hearing on Monday.

"Automating AI research is now the primary goal of these companies. It's what they're really gunning for. At my last job, I was in some sense working to automate myself. When I was at OpenAI, we had milestones for an automated AI researcher around 2027 or 2028, and we are on track or beating these expectations. That's a matter of months from now, not decades, or even five years. Once AI research is automated, humans will be much further out of the loop than we are today.

And today is already not great. I can tell you firsthand that the majority of the code is now written by AI, and people do not check it that carefully anymore."

selectedTweets.text:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: New York City subpoenaed four AI labs. Only three showed up.

• SpaceXAI did not attend, in direct violation of the subpoena, and the council says it will pursue the matter in court
• Anthropic sent Logan Graham, who runs the Frontier Red Team
• OpenAI sent Morgan Dwyer, head of policy development and operations, who was chief strategy officer implementing the CHIPS Act at Biden's Commerce Department
• Google sent its director of AI and emerging tech policy, Alice Friend. Meta sent its AI policy director for legislation, Shane Cahill
• Three of the four labs sent policy and legislative affairs people, so Anthropic was the only one that sent a researcher
• Speaker Julie Menin: "The idea that artificial intelligence is going to self-regulate defies all reason"

@theojaffee: "It's very strange that SpaceXAI did not send anyone. Why would they not do that?"

selectedTweets.bestBit: fine AI vendors $25K per unvalidated sale or deployment
selectedTweets.text:
Ex-Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon told New York City lawmakers that humans will probably lose control of AI and is set to testify at NYC AI hearing on ‘kill switches,’

New York City is also prepareing a bill that would require every AI model sold locally to pass outside validation first and would fine AI vendors $25K per unvalidated sale or deployment.

All 51 council members are weighing this lead bill that would outlaw marketing, selling or deploying any AI model in the city without outside validation. 

It also requires a shutdown capability, meaning a human operator can technically make the model stop working, temporarily or permanently. 

Validators would grade accuracy, calibration, determinism, latency, data provenance, bias, privacy and safety, then certify readiness to the city's Cyber Command.
